title: Loading-Dependent Osteogenic Performance of Core-Shell Nanocomposite-Reinforced Poly(ε-caprolactone) Scaffolds for Bone Regeneration.
abstract: Bone defect repair remains challenging due to the complex biological processes involving inflammation, angiogenesis, and osteogenesis. Although therapeutic ions and natural antioxidants have been individually investigated for bone regeneration, the biological performance of scaffolds incorporating multiple functional components at different loading contents remains to be fully explored. In this study, we designed a core-shell nanocomposite (GaTe-MBG@Cur-ZIF-8) consisting of Ga/Te-codoped mesoporous bioactive glass (GaTe-MBG) as the core and curcumin-loaded ZIF-8 as the shell. The nanocomposite was incorporated into poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) at different contents (0, 5, 10, and 15 wt %) to fabricate three-dimensional (3D)-printed composite scaffolds. The designed scaffolds were intended to provide a multifunctional platform integrating curcumin with Ga, Te, Zn, Si, and Ca ions. Among the investigated formulations, the scaffold containing 10% GaTe-MBG@Cur-ZIF-8 (by weight) exhibited the most favorable overall biological performance, including antioxidant activity, favorable inflammation-associated responses, enhanced osteogenic differentiation, and angiogenesis-related effects. In a rat cranial defect model, the 10% scaffold demonstrated improved bone regeneration compared to the other groups. RNA sequencing analysis revealed differential gene expression and enrichment of inflammation- and osteogenesis-related pathways, including IL-17, TNF, and MAPK signaling, suggesting potential associations between the scaffold-induced cellular responses and these signaling pathways. Collectively, these findings highlight the potential of the combined GaTe-MBG@Cur-ZIF-8 nanocomposite for bone tissue engineering and identify 10% as a favorable loading content within the investigated range, providing insights into the design of multifunctional composite scaffolds for bone regeneration.

title: Engineering mRNA-Lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines against multidrug resistant bacteria: current and future prospects.
abstract: This review highlights the significant potential of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technology for application in bacterial vaccines, with a long-term goal to provide critical tools in controlling problematic microbial infections regardless of their antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profile. The current landscape of bacterial vaccine development, including methods for identification of candidate antigens, are discussed along with emerging design principles for LNP delivery systems. We focus on mRNA-LNP systems for delivery of bacterial vaccine antigens in large part due to their extensive clinical validation, compatibility with reverse vaccinology, and growing prominence in modern vaccinology. Attention is also given to emerging opportunities to develop effective tools to combat severe infections, particularly those caused by AMR bacterial infections. Specific advantages and challenges of RNA-based vaccine platforms and LNP delivery systems compared to other vaccine modalities including strategies are highlighted, with a focus on particular strengths in conserved antigen identification via genome sequencing and recent advances in optimizing LNP composition for induction of strongly protective immunity for vaccine delivery. We argue that mRNA-LNP technology combined with reverse vaccinology approaches has the potential to improve and accelerate bacterial vaccine development, particularly for broadly protective immunity less dependent on bacterial strain surface composition and which are entirely dependent on host immunity, making them agnostic to the issue of antimicrobial resistance.

title: CHD4 promotes hepatitis B virus transcription by facilitating RNA polymerase II recruitment to cccDNA.
abstract: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global health burden, largely due to the persistence of covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), which serves as the template for viral transcription. Although host factors involved in regulating cccDNA transcription have been increasingly recognized, the molecular mechanisms controlling HBV minichromosome activity remain incompletely understood. Chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein 4 (CHD4), the catalytic component of the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase (NuRD) complex, is a key regulator of chromatin remodeling and transcriptional regulation. In this study, we demonstrate that CHD4 facilitates efficient HBV transcription. Depletion of CHD4 in HBV-infected hepatoma cells markedly reduced viral RNA levels and antigen production without affecting HBV uptake, nuclear import, cccDNA establishment, or cccDNA stability. Mechanistically, CHD4 was recruited to HBV cccDNA and promoted the occupancy of RNA polymerase II (RNA Pol II) on the viral minichromosome. Loss of CHD4 impaired RNA Pol II recruitment to cccDNA, resulting in reduced viral transcription. Furthermore, domain mapping identified the CT2 region of CHD4 as essential for its interaction with RNA Pol II. Collectively, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role of CHD4 in regulating HBV cccDNA transcription and establish CHD4-mediated RNA Pol II recruitment as a critical mechanism controlling HBV gene expression.IMPORTANCEHepatitis B virus (HBV) infection affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide and can lead to severe liver diseases, including cirrhosis and liver cancer. A major challenge in curing HBV infection is the persistence of a stable viral DNA structure inside infected liver cells that continuously produces viral components. Understanding how this viral DNA is controlled by host cells is essential for developing new therapeutic strategies. In this study, we identified chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein 4 (CHD4) as a host factor that supports HBV gene production by helping the virus recruit the cellular machinery required for viral RNA synthesis. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism by which human liver cells regulate HBV persistence and provide new insights into virus-host interactions that may guide future approaches to achieve durable HBV control.

title: Irisin alleviates oxidative stress and osteoblast apoptosis in glucocorticoid-induced rat osteonecrosis of the femoral head via the integrin αVβ5/Bach1/Nrf2 signaling pathway.
abstract: Glucocorticoid (GC)‑induced osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH) is associated with oxidative stress and osteoblast apoptosis. Irisin, the cleaved form of fibronectin type III domain‑containing protein 5, attenuates oxidative stress and apoptosis in numerous types of cells, including osteoblasts, osteocytes and cardiomyocytes. The present study aimed to investigate the role of irisin and the mechanism behind GC‑induced ONFH in vivo, as well as oxidative stress and osteoblast apoptosis in vitro. In the present study, GC‑induced ONFH was established in rats by intramuscular injection of methylprednisolone, with irisin administered by intraperitoneal injection; the FHs were then assessed by micro‑CT, histology, immunohistochemistry and TUNEL staining. In vitro, murine osteoblastic MC3T3‑E1 cells were treated with dexamethasone (DEX), and oxidative stress, apoptosis and Nrf2 signaling were evaluated by dihydroethidium/JC‑1 staining, flow cytometry, reverse transcription‑quantitative PCR and western blotting. Irisin prevented the development of GC‑induced ONFH in rats, and alleviated oxidative stress and apoptosis in DEX‑treated osteoblasts. To determine the underlying mechanisms by which irisin exerted beneficial effects on DEX‑treated osteoblasts, the present study investigated Nrf2 signaling cascades. Irisin induced Nrf2 signaling cascade activation in MC3T3‑E1 cells and Nrf2 silencing by targeted short hairpin RNA reversed the beneficial effects of irisin on DEX‑treated osteoblasts. Further mechanistic analysis revealed that irisin physically interacted with integrin (ITG) αVβ5 on osteoblasts, activating Erk1 signaling. This activation promoted nuclear export of Bach1, a competitive suppressor of Nrf2, thereby relieving Bach1‑mediated suppression of antioxidant response elements. Consequently, irisin enhanced Nrf2 nuclear accumulation and upregulated its target genes [heme oxygenase, NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1, glutamate‑cysteine ligase catalytic subunit], reducing reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial membrane potential loss. Pharmacological inhibition of ITG αVβ5 or Erk1/2 abolished irisin‑induced Bach1 export, Nrf2 activation and cytoprotective effects. Collectively, the present study indicated that irisin may mitigate GC‑induced ONFH and osteoblast apoptosis via the ITG αVβ5/Bach1/Nrf2 signaling pathway, highlighting its therapeutic potential.

title: PRMT1 blockade reverts resistance to KRAS (G12C) inhibition through modulating ferroptosis signalling.
abstract: While Kirsten rat sarcoma virus (KRAS) G12C inhibitors (KRAS G12Ci) are successful in clinical practice, their long‑term efficacy is limited by acquired resistance, and effective combination strategies are urgently needed. In the present study, pancreatic and lung cancer cell lines resistant to KRAS G12Ci (AMG510/D‑1553) were established. Ribonucleic acid‑sequencing (RNA‑seq) identified significant alterations in ferroptosis‑related signaling in KRAS G12Ci‑resistant cells. Through in vivo and in vitro experiments, it was found that an increase occurred in the expression level of protein arginine methyltransferase 1 (PRMT1) in resistant cells. The combined inhibition of KRAS G12C and PRMT1 showed a stronger inhibitory effect on tumor growth than single‑target inhibition. Mechanistically, the inhibition of PRMT1 could make histone H4 at arginine 3 (H4R3me2a) less enriched in the promoter region of solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11). This suggests that PRMT1 may promote the transcription of SLC7A11 via epigenetic regulation mediated by H4R3me2a. Thus, this inhibits ferroptosis and potentially contributes to the maintenance of the KRAS G12Ci‑resistant phenotype. In summary, elevated PRMT1 expression was associated with KRAS G12C inhibitor resistance, and pharmacological inhibition of PRMT1‑associated activity enhanced the efficacy of KRAS G12C inhibition partly through ferroptosis. Further genetic validation is required to establish the specific role of PRMT1. The results of the present study will provide new targets and a theoretical basis for overcoming KRAS‑targeted treatment resistance, and will also promote the clinical translation of combined therapy.

title: The complete mitochondrial genome of Pseudocercospora zelkovae (Mycosphaerellaceae, Mycosphaerellales).
abstract: Pseudocercospora zelkovae is an ascomycete fungus that has been reported as a causal agent of leaf spot on Zelkova serrata in several East Asian countries, including South Korea. In this study, the complete mitochondrial genome of P. zelkovae was characterized through de novo assembly using Illumina sequencing data. The mitochondrial genome is a circular molecule of 33,324 bp with a GC content of 27.87%. It comprises a total of 41 genes, comprising 14 protein-coding genes, 25 transfer RNA genes, and two ribosomal RNA genes. Phylogenetic analysis of the protein-coding sequences from the mitochondrial genome revealed a close relationship between P. zelkovae and other Cercosporoid fungi including P. mori and P. fuligena within the Mycosphaerellaceae family.

title: Complete mitochondrial genomes of the highly invasive ant Paratrechina longicornis Latreille (Hymenoptera: Formicidae).
abstract: Paratrechina longicornis (Latreille), widely transported across subtropical and tropical regions, is frequently detected during plant quarantine inspections in South Korea and commonly found in port areas. It thrives in both disturbed and undisturbed habitats as a general scavenger, with nests typically established in dry litter, mulch or beneath ground objects. The specimens were collected in Vietnam through the efforts of an international joint research team. The complete mitogenome of P. longicornis was sequenced, assembled and annotated. The mitogenome of P. longicornis is a circular DNA molecule of 19,102 bp with an A + T content of 80.87%, comprising 13 protein-coding genes, 22 transfer RNA genes and 2 ribosomal RNA genes. Phylogenetic analysis showed that P. longicornis clustered with Acropyga, Anoplolepsis, Formica, Lasius, Nylanderia and Camponotus species in the well-supported subfamily Formicinae.

title: Complete chloroplast genome sequence data of Morus nigra L.
abstract: Morus nigra L. is a black mulberry species with high medicinal and ornamental value. Its complete chloroplast genome was obtained using a combination of Illumina and Oxford Nanopore high-throughput sequencing platforms. The circular chloroplast genome of M. nigra is 159,330 bp in length with a GC content of 36.15%. It consists of a large single-copy (LSC) region of 88,104 bp, a small single-copy (SSC) region of 19,870 bp, and two inverted repeat (IR) regions (IRa and IRb) of 25,678 bp each. The chloroplast genome contains 130 genes, including 85 protein-coding genes, 37 transfer RNA (tRNA) genes, and eight ribosomal RNA (rRNA) genes. A total of 451 simple sequence repeat (SSR) loci were identified, among which dinucleotide repeats were the most dominant (219 loci, 48.6%). Phylogenetic analysis based on the chloroplast genomes of 27 species showed that all Morus species formed a monophyletic clade, with M. nigra occupying an independent branch. These data expand the genetic resources available for Morus and provide a foundation for future studies on the development and utilization of this species.

title: Complete mitochondrial genome of Rhopalaea crassa (Ascidiacea, Aplousobranchia, Diazonidae) and phylogenetic analysis.
abstract: In this study, we determined the complete mitochondrial genome of Rhopalaea crassa (Herdman 1880), a solitary ascidian belonging to the family Diazonidae. The mitochondrial genome of R. crassa is 15,413 bp in length, containing 13 protein-coding genes, 24 transfer RNA genes, and two ribosomal RNA genes. The mitochondrial gene arrangement of R. crassa differs from those reported from previously sequenced Aplousobranchia mitogenomes. Phylogenetic analyses based on concatenated protein-coding genes consistently recovered R. crassa as the sister species of R. idoneta within Diazonidae, with strong support from both Maximum Likelihood and Bayesian Inference analyses.

title: TRPM2-mediated Ca2+ entry drives cellular senescence to irradiation-induced salivary gland dysfunction.
abstract: Aberrant Ca2+ signaling, mediated by multiple ion channels, is increasingly recognized as a central driver of irradiation-induced salivary gland dysfunction; however, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly defined. Here, we identify the transient receptor potential melastatin-2 (TRPM2) channel as a key mediator of irradiation-induced Ca2+ entry that drives salivary gland dysfunction. Trpm2 -/- mice were resistant to irradiation-induced salivary gland dysfunction at the acute/early stage of post-irradiation. RNA sequence analysis further showed that cell cycle pathways were upregulated, along with a decrease in ROS and its associated pathways in irradiated Trpm2 -/- mice. Mechanistically, our data show that loss of TRPM2 decreases cellular senescence, restores mitochondrial Ca2+ handling and bioenergetics, along with DNA repair and protein synthesis. Finally, we show that pharmacological inhibition of senescence with quercetin or piperlongumine prevents irradiation-induced salivary gland dysfunction. Together, our findings provide a mechanistic link between TRPM2-dependent Ca2+ signaling and cellular senescence as a key driver of irradiation-induced salivary gland dysfunction.

title: Messenger RNA vaccines and beyond: Molecular design, delivery platforms, and emerging therapeutic applications.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) medicine has progressed from a conceptual nucleic acid modality to a clinically validated platform for transient protein expression, with SARS-CoV-2 vaccines providing population-scale proof of maturity. This review synthesizes the molecular and translational principles underlying this transition, emphasizing two determinants of mRNA performance: transcript engineering and delivery formulation. Transcript engineering integrates cap structure, untranslated regions, coding-sequence optimization, nucleoside chemistry, and poly(A) design, whereas formulation controls encapsulation, tissue tropism, cytosolic release, stability, and route-dependent biodistribution. We examine how this platform logic extends beyond vaccination to protein replacement, lung-directed gene complementation, regenerative signaling, in vivo antibody production, local tumor immunomodulation, genome editing, and transient ex vivo cell engineering. We also compare conventional mRNA, self-amplifying RNA, and circular RNA as complementary architectures with distinct dose requirements, expression durability, immunogenicity, and manufacturability. Across preventive and therapeutic settings, translation is constrained by extrahepatic delivery specificity, productive endosomal escape, innate and carrier-driven immune responses during repeat dosing, and scalable manufacturing with robust analytical quality control. The future of mRNA medicine will depend on platform matching: aligning RNA architecture, formulation, administration route, and disease context with clinical settings in which transient expression offers a genuine therapeutic advantage.

title: Design and applications of engineering coronavirus vaccines with virus-like particles.
abstract: Coronavirus vaccine development must accommodate antigenic evolution, diverse host species, and the distinct immune demands of respiratory and enteric disease. Virus-like particles (VLPs) are genome-free particulate immunogens that present coronavirus antigens in a defined structural context without productive infection. This review differentiates authentic coronavirus-mimetic VLPs containing spike (S), envelope (E), membrane (M), and nucleocapsid (N) proteins; simplified envelope-based VLPs; and heterologous scaffolds displaying S-derived antigens. We examine how production platforms shape product attributes, how preassembled particles can complement messenger RNA vaccines, and how antigen composition, adjuvant, and administration route influence humoral, cellular, and mucosal immunity. Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) provides the most advanced translational evidence, including protective animal studies, phase III efficacy, and regulatory authorization of a plant-derived VLP vaccine. Evidence from SARS-CoV, Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus, and veterinary coronaviruses extends the rationale, especially for multivalent coverage, maternal immunity, and repeated vaccination. The key question is whether VLP complexity provides a measurable immunological or deployment advantage for a defined use case. Progress will require scalable manufacture, rigorous structural characterization, comparability after antigen updates, and efficacy endpoints aligned with host and virus biology.

title: Programmable RNA therapeutics: converging vaccination and on-demand disease treatment via self-adaptive RNA platforms.
abstract: RNA technology, most prominently messenger RNA (mRNA), has transformed vaccine development by enabling rapid, sequence-specific antigen design, scalable manufacturing, and transient protein expression. Its long-term significance, however, extends beyond prophylactic vaccination. This Perspective argues that mRNA should be conceptualised as a programmable therapeutic platform capable of integrating vaccination, immune modulation, and on-demand disease treatment. Current mRNA vaccines deliver predefined antigenic instructions, whereas emerging RNA systems, including self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA, sequence-engineered mRNA, and targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), may support more adaptable therapeutic functions. Such platforms could prime immunity, replace deficient proteins, encode antibodies, reprogramme immune cells, or induce antigen-specific tolerance. The concept of self-adaptive RNA-based therapeutics remains at an early stage and should not be overstated; most existing systems are programmable at the design stage rather than biologically autonomous after administration. Nonetheless, this conceptual position is no longer purely speculative: the first regulatory approval of a self-amplifying RNA vaccine and controlled-trial evidence of clinical benefit from a personalised neoantigen mRNA therapeutic in resected melanoma indicate that programmable RNA platforms are beginning to move from concept to clinical validation across both the prophylactic and therapeutic ends of the spectrum. Key challenges include tissue-specific delivery, expression control, innate immune activation, repeat dosing, safety assessment, regulatory classification, and equitable access. A self-adaptive RNA-based framework does not replace existing vaccines or biologics but extends them towards responsive, personalised, and temporally controlled therapy.

title: Antiviral mechanism of glycyrrhizic acid against BVDV: suppression of viral replication and immune regulation.
abstract: Bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV), a globally prevalent pathogen in cattle, causes severe economic losses through acute diarrhea, immunosuppression, and reproductive failure, with mortality rates reaching 20%-30% in persistently infected herds. This study investigated glycyrrhizic acid (GA), a bioactive triterpenoid glycoside derived from licorice root with known anti-inflammatory and broad-spectrum antiviral properties, as a potential inhibitor of BVDV replication. Using in vitro (MDBK cells) and in vivo (BALB/c mice) models, we evaluated the antiviral and immunomodulatory effects of GA. Cells were treated with 10 μM GA, and mice received 20 mg/kg/day GA. Viral replication, cytokine expression, hepatic histopathology, and gut microbiota were assessed. GA treatment significantly reduced BVDV replication, decreasing 5'UTR and NS5B mRNA expression by >80% (P < 0.01) and viral titers by 2.3-log in liver tissue. GA concurrently modulated host immune responses, suppressing pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α by 68%, IL-6 by 54%) while elevating IL-10 (2.1-fold), and substantially improved hepatic histopathology scores (P < 0.05 versus infected controls). ELISA revealed GA-mediated downregulation of IFN-β during infection. Analysis of gut microbiota at 7 days post-infection revealed that both GA and ribavirin (RBV) treatments modulated microbial community structure, with RBV showing profiles more closely resembling uninfected controls. These findings establish GA's dual antiviral mechanism-direct suppression of viral RNA synthesis and immunomodulation-positioning this natural compound as a promising therapeutic candidate against BVDV infection in livestock.

title: Engineered compact TnpB epigenetic editors prevent choroidal neovascularization via Vegfa repression.
abstract: Epigenetic editing enables programmable and heritable gene regulation without altering DNA sequence, yet existing platforms remain constrained by large size, cumbersome target design, and limited applicability. Here we engineered catalytically inactive ISDge10 and ISAam1 TnpB systems and developed highly compact RNA-guided epigenetic editors compatible with single adeno-associated virus (AAV) delivery for either transcriptional activation or repression. Activators based on these TnpBs (Dge10on and Aam1on) efficiently activated diverse endogenous genes in vitro, and AAV9-delivered Aam1on achieved robust pancreatic and duodenal homeobox 1 (Pdx1) activation in vivo. For gene repression, by screening 248 human Krüppel-associated box (KRAB) domains with verified effector activity, we identified the most potent effector domain for each TnpB system, resulting in the optimization of Dge10off and Aam1off. These epigenetic editors mediated durable transcriptional repression across multiple loci in diverse cell types. In a mouse model, single-AAV delivery of these editors efficiently suppressed vascular endothelial growth factor A (Vegfa) expression with no detectable activation of DNA damage response markers (γH2AX and p53), resulting in marked reductions in choroidal neovascularization area. Our study expands the epigenetic editing toolbox and provides a potentially safe and durable single-administration therapeutic strategy for wet age-related macular degeneration (wAMD).

title: A p32 family RNA editing factor acts in mitochondrial ribosome biogenesis.
abstract: Biogenesis of mitochondrial ribosomes (mitoribosomes) in the unicellular parasite Trypanosoma brucei requires an exceptionally large toolkit of assembly factors, identified in stable precursors of large and small mitoribosomal subunits (mtLSU and mtSSU) by cryoEM. Here, using genetic modifications and proteomic characterization of the immunoprecipitated assemblosome, the earliest characterized mtSSU precursor, we determined that a cap of its distinctive protrusion of hitherto unknown composition consists of a p22 homotrimer. This protein was previously implicated in the uridine-insertion editing of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit II transcript. Our functional analysis confirmed this role but revealed that its ablation also causes a loss of mtSSU and a systemic reduction in mitochondrial translation, phenocopying the depletion of established mitoribosomal assembly factors. Consequently, the oxidative phosphorylation system and mitochondrial function are compromised. The p22 protein belongs to the p32 family. We showed that five of its six trypanosomal members are involved in mtSSU biogenesis. Notably, p32 proteins are associated with mitoribosomes in two other distant eukaryotic lineages. A eukaryote-wide mapping of p32 proteins documented that their presence correlates with the retention of mitochondrial genomes. Together, our findings redefine trypanosomal p22 as a dual-function coordinator of mitochondrial gene expression and reveal that the ancestral role of the p32 family is associated with mitochondrial translation.

title: GSH/pH Dual-Responsive Zwitterionic mRNA Nanocomplexes for Tumor-Enriched mRNA Delivery in a B16F10 Melanoma Model.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapy offers a programmable route to melanoma treatment, but its translation is limited by nuclease degradation, off-target biodistribution and endolysosomal trapping. Here we report a glutathione (GSH)/pH dual-responsive mRNA nanocomplex (mRNA-NC) fabricated by one-pot in situ polymerization of N-(3-aminopropyl)methacrylamide (APMA), 1-vinylimidazole (VI), N,N'-bis(acryloyl)cystamine (BACA), and 2-methacryloyloxyethyl phosphorylcholine (MPC) on the mRNA template. At an N/P ratio of 40, the carrier reached an encapsulation efficiency of 92.7 ± 2.1% and a loading capacity of 87.4 ± 3.2 μg mg-1, forming monodisperse particles of 126.4 ± 7.2 nm (polydispersity index, PDI, 0.14). The zwitterionic corona limited plasma protein adsorption to 12.6 ± 1.5 μg mg-1 (4.6-fold lower than jetPEI/mRNA), kept hemolysis at 0.8 ± 0.2%, and extended the serum half-life of the mRNA to ≈27.4 h, roughly 9-fold longer than naked mRNA. Release was gated by both triggers: 86.5 ± 3.7% of the cargo was released within 8 h under 10 mM GSH, whereas leakage under physiological conditions remained ≤ 12%; in a 4 h matrix, pH 5.5 plus 10 mM GSH released 85 ± 6.8% versus 12 ± 1.5% at pH 7.4 without GSH. In B16F10 cells, the nanocomplex was taken up in a dose- and energy-dependent manner, entered the lysosomal compartment, and escaped over time in a manner consistent with imidazole-mediated proton-sponge buffering (a hypothesis; intralysosomal pH was not measured directly), producing a peak firefly luciferase (FLuc) expression of 56,140 ± 3280 RLU mg-1 protein at 24 h, about 1.5-fold higher than jetPEI/mRNA, with 93.6 ± 3.9% cell viability and 6.7 ± 1.2% lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release. In B16F10-bearing albino C57BL/6 mice, a single intravenous dose produced tumor-dominant bioluminescence (peak 5.7 × 106 photons s-1 at 6 h), a tumor enrichment index of 1.22 ± 0.18 (vs 0.31 ± 0.03 for jetPEI/mRNA) and 2.42 × 107 FLuc mRNA copies μg-1 tumor RNA at 12 h, while all 7-day safety indicators remained at phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) levels. These results demonstrate that a single zwitterionic nanocomplex can integrate stealth, dual-triggered release, and endosomal escape for safe, tumor-enriched mRNA delivery. While this study focuses on delivery performance and reporter gene expression, it lays a solid foundation for future therapeutic applications with functional mRNA.

title: PIANO enables generative modeling of gene expression and scales multi-omics integration to 100 million cells.
abstract: Single-cell RNA technologies enable the routine acquisition of transcriptomic atlases. However, these molecular profiles are influenced by overlapping sources of variation. Since these covariates confound comparisons, data integration is the first step in most analyses. Three challenges remain: correcting strong batch effects, scaling to millions of cells, and modeling how covariates influence gene expression. To address these challenges, we developed PIANO, probabilistic inference autoencoder networks for multi-omics, a deep learning framework whose central feature is a generative model of gene expression data. Additionally, PIANO achieves robust integrations and trains 10× faster than previous methods. PIANO accurately integrates single-cell data across species and across single-cell and spatial transcriptomics modalities. As practical applications, PIANO models spatially resolved gene expression during Alzheimer's disease progression in human brains and integrates over 100 million cancer cells to model drug perturbations. In summary, PIANO's integration and generative modeling capabilities will empower novel insights for a wide range of future studies.

title: Coupled RNA editing and splicing within plant chloroplasts by the MORFs-CFM2 interaction module.
abstract: RNA editing and splicing are two important post-transcriptional processing steps in plant chloroplasts. Evidence gathered in recent years indicates that these two steps are often tightly connected, although the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Here, we elucidate that the splicing protein CFM2 is associated with the MORF2/MORF9 editors and is involved in editing-splicing coupling within plant chloroplasts. Using immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS) and in vitro/in vivo interaction assays, we identified the chloroplast splicing factor CFM2 as a direct physical interactor of the core editosome components MORF2 and MORF9. Disruption of CFM2 in Arabidopsis thaliana results in an albino-lethal phenotype, accompanied not only by impaired splicing of specific group II introns (e.g., ycf3.1, ndhA, and ndhB) but also by severe defects in RNA editing across multiple chloroplast sites, phenocopying morf2 and morf9 mutants. Conversely, mutations in the MORF genes analogously compromise splicing efficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this mechanistic coupling is evolutionarily conserved between dicots and monocots, as loss of the rice homolog OsCFM2 drastically impairs site-specific editing. Together, our findings provide compelling evidence that, the MORF-CFM2 complex forms a physical association, coordinating the dual maturation of chloroplast transcripts to ensure photosynthetic function and plant viability.

title: mRNA-LNP vaccines targeting mutation-derived BRCA2 and p53 elicit antigen-specific immune responses in beagles.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines are next-generation platforms capable of eliciting potent cellular and humoral immunity through intracellular expression of tumor-associated or mutation-specific antigens. Canine mammary gland tumor (CMT), commonly encountered in female dogs, frequently harbors mutations in the BRCA2 and p53 genes, which are also relevant to human breast cancers. We aimed to design mutation-targeted mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines encoding canine BRCA2 and p53 variants using in silico epitope prediction and evaluate their immunogenicity and safety. Three mRNA constructs encoding BRCA2 and p53 mutations were synthesized and encapsulated in ionizable-lipid-based LNPs. The resulting mRNA-LNP formulations, namely canine BRCA2-10204ins candidates (cBR2-Cand), canine BRCA2-p53 28-mer epitopes (cBR2-p53), and canine BRCA2-partial (cBR2-Part), were then admixed to prepare the cBR2-cocktail, a mixed mRNA-LNP vaccine designed to enhance mutation-specific immune responses. In vitro expression was confirmed in HeLa cells. In vivo immunization in mice induced strong interferon (IFN)-γ secretion, particularly against BRCA2 H143R, K801R, and T1425P mutations. Beagles immunized with cBR2-cocktail mRNA-LNPs exhibited increased IFN-γ production in peripheral blood mononuclear cells after repeated dosing, without significant hematological or biochemical abnormalities. Mutation-derived mRNA-LNP vaccines safely induced mutation-specific T-cell responses in vivo. Although anticancer efficacy was not assessed, we established a preclinical foundation for developing mutation-targeted mRNA immunotherapies for CMT and underscored the translational relevance of the canine model for human BRCA2/p53-related cancers.

title: The hypoxia, lactate and lactylation axis in lung disease: A metabolic and epigenetic framework.
abstract: Hypoxia accompanies diverse pulmonary diseases and can promote glycolytic reprogramming and lactate accumulation. Lactate serves as a metabolic fuel and signalling molecule and can supply substrates for protein lysine lactylation. These activities are related but experimentally distinct. Here, we evaluate a hypoxia, lactate and lactylation framework across pulmonary hypertension, lung cancer, pulmonary fibrosis, acute lung injury, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma. We distinguish studies that manipulate oxygen availability and measure downstream metabolic and lactylation responses from those that demonstrate lactate signalling or lactylation without establishing hypoxia as the initiating event. We assess evidence for individual mechanisms according to human validation, biochemical resolution and the specificity of in vivo interventions. This comparison identifies substantial gaps between an observed metabolic sequence and proof that a particular lactylation event mediates disease. We also examine how protein lactylation intersects with RNA-modifying enzymes and DNA-repair machinery, while recognizing that direct nucleic-acid lactylation remains unvalidated. Potential interventions range from lactate production and transport to lactylation regulators, but current agents frequently alter metabolism or other protein acylations. The framework therefore provides a basis for testing how oxygen stress influences pulmonary pathology rather than evidence for a uniformly established causal pathway or a clinically validated therapeutic class.

title: Richness and prevalence matching weakens variable-selection contrasts between low-abundance and abundant bacteria in aged-landfill refuse.
abstract: Aged municipal solid waste (MSW) forms a heterogeneous biogeochemical matrix, which complicates the use of biological indicators for assessing landfill stabilization. Low-abundance bacteria in this matrix may represent genuine, localized refuse niches; however, singletons, doubletons, and unequal amplicon sequence variant (ASV) richness among samples can inflate apparent diversity and promote over-interpretation. We tested whether low-abundance bacteria add ecological information to aged-refuse microbiomes, analyzing 18 MSW samples from seven landfill sites by 16S ribosomal RNA gene amplicon sequencing with sites as regional units. At the sample-level, rare fractions harbored higher detected richness and diversity than abundant fractions, even though the 0.01 % cutoff represented only one or two reads at the ∼ 23,000-read rarefaction depth. The two fractions nevertheless exhibited distinct taxonomic profiles. Assembly analysis initially suggested stronger variable selection in recurrent low-abundance ASVs than in abundant ASVs (41.8 % versus 22.2 % of pairs), but three matching schemes attenuated this contrast: the excess reflected richness and prevalence structure, not fraction-specific determinism. After matching, variable-selection proportions fell to 10.3-14.4 % and overlapped the abundant comparator under all schemes and aggregation scopes. PICRUSt2 predictions showed a parallel pattern: rare fractions contained more predicted Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes orthologs overall but fewer per ASV, and their ASVs were further from sequenced reference genomes (all P < 0.0001). Recurrent low-abundance taxa are best viewed as candidates for targeted validation-exemplified by Syntrophomonas and Dethiobacter-not as evidence of intrinsic variable-selection tendency or functional activity. This tiered framework supports microbial candidate selection for validation against direct stabilization measurements.

title: CTCF regulates wild-type and recombinant AAV gene expression by shaping viral chromatin.
abstract: Adeno-Associated Viruses (AAVs) are powerful platforms for delivering therapeutic transgenes via recombinant AAV (rAAV) vectors. However, a limited understanding of the regulation of AAV gene expression has narrowed the ability to efficiently express therapeutic transgenes from rAAV vectors. Since rAAVs retain only the wtAAV inverted terminal repeats (ITR), we hypothesized that regulatory elements outside the ITR that govern wild-type AAV (wtAAV) gene expression can be used to modify rAAV genomes to enhance vector performance. Through in silico analysis, biochemical pulldowns, and high-throughput sequencing, we have identified that the host architectural protein CCCTC-binding Factor (CTCF) associates with the wtAAV type 2 (wtAAV2) genome but is absent from rAAV vectors. Global knockdown and site-specific deletion revealed that the CTCF binding element (CBE) on the wtAAV2 genome, located upstream of the viral P5 promoter, regulates expression of the viral Rep68/78 genes. We have re-engineered new rAAV vectors expressing a GFP reporter transgene to contain the wtAAV2-CBE upstream of the vector promoter. Our results show that CTCF binding dramatically increased rAAV transduction efficiency and GFP expression by up to four-fold across multiple cell types. This enhancement was independent of the AAV capsid serotype used for packaging rAAV vectors. CUT&RUN analysis revealed that this CBE was necessary and sufficient to regulate the chromatin landscape of wtAAV2 and rAAV2. Finally, we observed that CTCF-mediated chromatin remodeling of rAAV2 led to increased production of nascent RNA transcripts from the vector genome. Based on our findings, we propose that CTCF supports wtAAV2/rAAV gene expression by shaping the local chromatin landscape.

title: The LiCO platform: A novel benzimidazole-based lipid conjugate for versatile and sustained siRNA delivery beyond the liver.
abstract: Extending oligonucleotide therapeutics beyond the liver remains a central challenge for RNA medicine. Here, we describe a lipid-conjugated oligonucleotide (LiCO), a benzimidazole-enabled lipid-duplex RNA conjugate platform synthesized as a single chemical entity by standard solid-phase chemistry. Structure-activity screening identified a 5'-passenger-strand hexadecyl (C16) conjugate whose benzimidazole (SDL) linker markedly improved delivery activity relative to a linker-free analog, and studies in CD36-knockout mice established CD36-dependent uptake as the principal driver of extrahepatic tropism. A single systemic dose in mice produced >90% target knockdown in skeletal muscle, heart, aorta, and adipose tissue, with ≥50% silencing persisting for 6 months and measurable activity at 9 months, whereas hepatic silencing was transient. In cynomolgus macaques, two intravenous doses of LiCO-siMSTN achieved ∼90% myostatin mRNA knockdown, 60%-70% suppression of circulating myostatin protein through day 98, and progressive muscle hypertrophy without adverse clinical, hematological, or biochemical findings. In situ hybridization confirmed deep penetration of myofibers, myocardium, and aortic smooth muscle. LiCO also enabled potent local delivery to the synovium, retina, and bladder with minimal systemic exposure. LiCO offers a scalable, versatile platform for neuromuscular, metabolic, and localized disorders.

title: Role and mechanism of ribosomal protein S3 in tyrosine kinase inhibitor resistance in chronic myeloid leukemia.
abstract: Resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) remains a major cause of treatment failure in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). This study investigated the role of ribosomal protein S3 (RPS3) in TKI resistance and its association with NF-κB signaling. Exploratory RNA sequencing and an RNA-binding protein database were used to prioritize a candidate for subsequent clinical expression and functional analyses. RPS3 expression was examined in an independent clinical cohort and resistant cell models. RPS3 knockdown and pharmacological modulation were used to evaluate drug sensitivity, apoptosis, cell cycle distribution, and NF-κB-associated signaling. RPS3 was upregulated in clinical samples from patients with TKI resistance or poor responses and in resistant cell models. Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed that RPS3 expression discriminated between resistant/poor-response patients and good responders in the validation cohort. RPS3 knockdown lowered imatinib and nilotinib IC50 values, with increased apoptosis and G0/G1-phase arrest following TKI exposure. These effects were accompanied by reduced p65 phosphorylation, a lower p65 nuclear/cytoplasmic fluorescence ratio, and decreased MCL-1 and BCL-XL mRNA levels. TNF-α treatment increased TKI tolerance and reduced TKI-induced apoptosis in RPS3-knockdown cells, whereas co-treatment with BAY-11-7082 counteracted these effects. BAY-11-7082 also showed synergistic inhibitory effects with TKIs in resistant cells under the highest single agent model. These findings identify RPS3 as a contributor to TKI resistance in CML cell models and connect its functional effects to NF-κB-associated anti-apoptotic signaling. By integrating clinical expression data with functional and pharmacological analyses, this study supports further investigation of RPS3 as a candidate target for sensitizing resistant CML cells to TKIs.

title: Hypoxia-inducible factor-1α stabilized stem cells from human deciduous teeth in 3D spheroids promote endothelial differentiation and improve hindlimb ischemia.
abstract: Critical limb ischemia (CLI) remains a major clinical challenge with limited treatment options. This study explores a novel approach to enhance the therapeutic potential of stem cells from human exfoliated deciduous teeth (SHED) by combining hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) stabilization with 3D spheroid culture, with the aim of boosting endothelial differentiation and improving outcomes in a mouse model of CLI. SHED were transfected with small hairpin RNA (shRNA) targeting prolyl hydroxylase domain-containing protein 2 (PHD2) to stabilize HIF-1α, then self-assembled into 3D spheroids on non-adhesive microwells. Spheroid diameters of 200 μm, 400 μm, and 600 μm were tested for endothelial differentiation. After 7 days of 3D culture, spheroids were transferred to 2D culture dishes and maintained for an additional 7 days to obtain monodispersed Induced-SHED. Endothelial differentiation was assessed via qRT-PCR, western blotting, immunofluorescence, Matrigel tube formation, and RNA sequencing. Induced-SHED were encapsulated in fibrin hydrogel and injected into mice with surgically induced hindlimb ischemia (HLI). Therapeutic effects were evaluated by blood perfusion, ischemia scoring, immunohistochemistry, and Masson's trichrome staining. Statistical analysis used Student's t-test and one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test. PHD2 knockdown led to a sevenfold increase in HIF-1 expression without affecting proliferation. Spheroids of 400 μm in diameter exhibited the highest expression of endothelial markers (CD31, VEGFR2) at both the mRNA and protein levels and were identified as optimal for promoting endothelial differentiation. Induced-SHED formed robust vascular networks on Matrigel, with sprouting lengths significantly greater than controls and exhibited phenotypic and functional properties similar to those of endothelial cells in vitro. In vivo, HLI mice treated with Induced-SHED showed markedly improved blood perfusion, reduced ischemic scores, enhanced angiogenesis (as indicated by increased CD31 + vessels), and less muscle fibrosis compared with controls. RNA sequencing revealed upregulation of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1), which was shown to potentiate cell-extracellular matrix interactions, thereby inducing endothelial differentiation of SHED. The combination of HIF-1α stabilization and 3D spheroid culture significantly enhanced SHED endothelial differentiation and therapeutic potential in treating CLI.

title: Transient (Pro)renin receptor silencing disrupts proximal tubule development in human kidney organoids.
abstract: The (pro)renin receptor [(P)RR] plays a crucial role in murine kidney development, but its function in human kidneys remains poorly understood due to the lack of suitable research models. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived kidney organoids recapitulate early kidney development and are therefore suitable to investigate the effects of (P)RR knockdown on nephron formation in a human setting. Human iPSC were differentiated into kidney organoids, and (P)RR was silenced using small interfering RNA delivered by nucleofection either at the primitive streak stage or during nephron progenitor cell induction. Organoid development was evaluated morphologically and by analysis of nephron markers at the mRNA and protein levels. We found that transient silencing of (P)RR during primitive streak formation resulted in smaller organoids, impaired proximal tubule formation, increased stromal cell populations, and promoted fibrosis, while podocyte and distal tubule development remained unaffected. In contrast, transient (P)RR knockdown during nephron progenitor cell induction selectively disrupted proximal tubule formation without affecting organoid size or the development of podocytes and distal tubules. Our findings demonstrate a pivotal role for (P)RR in human kidney development. This contributes to our understanding of kidney development disorders and identifies (P)RR as a potential target for future genetic and therapeutic interventions in renal hypoplasia and hypodysplasia.
authors: Thierry P P van den Bosch

title: Human Multi-Omics Meta-Analysis Identifies Molecular Layer-Specific Responses to Resistance and Endurance Exercise.
abstract: Resistance and endurance exercise produce distinct adaptations, but molecular responses that distinguish these exercise modalities across studies and molecular layers remain incompletely defined. We sought to identify reproducible resistance- and endurance-associated molecular responses across human skeletal muscle and plasma omics datasets. We integrated publicly available human exercise omics datasets. Random-effects meta-analyses included 15,312 genes from three skeletal muscle RNA-seq datasets and 4,641 proteins from two skeletal muscle proteomic datasets. Early skeletal muscle phosphoproteomic responses were compared across two independent studies using 2,430 matched phosphosites. At 24 hours, skeletal muscle phosphoproteomics and targeted and untargeted metabolomics in skeletal muscle and plasma were analyzed separately; plasma proteomics was not analyzed. Effects were standardized as resistance exercise minus endurance exercise, with significance defined within each molecular layer at FDR<0.05. RNA-seq identified 269 genes, including 71 resistance-associated and 198 endurance-associated genes. Global proteomics identified 10 proteins (nine resistance-associated; one endurance-associated). Early phosphoproteomic effects correlated across studies (r=0.589, P=4.1x10-227); 210 of 238 significant phosphosites were directionally concordant, and 51 met replication criteria. At 24 hours, targeted plasma metabolomics identified 14 endurance-associated features, while untargeted plasma metabolomics identified 18 features, including nine resistance-associated and nine endurance-associated features. Resistance-associated responses involved contractile, myofibrillar, cytoskeletal, extracellular matrix, protein quality-control, stress-response, and phosphorylation-related processes. Endurance-associated responses involved mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, respiratory-chain biology, fatty acid oxidation, substrate utilization, amino acid metabolism, and mitochondrial proteostasis. Human molecular responses to resistance and endurance exercise are molecular-layer specific. Endurance-associated responses were more consistently represented in transcriptomic and metabolic layers, whereas resistance-associated responses were more prominent in protein abundance and phosphorylation. These findings provide a quantitative basis for selecting molecular measurements and sampling strategies in future human resistance and endurance exercise studies.

title: Massively Parallel, Ultra-accurate RNA Sequencing with CircSeq.
abstract: Accurate transcription of the human genome is essential for cellular health. However, it has been difficult to design tools that can accurately measure the fidelity of transcription in cellular systems. Here, we describe a protocol for CircSeq, a high-resolution next-generation sequencing method capable of detecting transcription errors in any transcript of any organism. Using rolling-circle reverse transcription, CircSeq generates multiple concatenated cDNA copies from a single circularized RNA fragment, allowing true transcription errors to be distinguished from random artifacts that arise during library preparation or sequencing. Using commercially available reagents and adaptable to diverse organisms and transcript types, CircSeq provides a robust and rigorous approach to quantifying the fidelity of whole transcriptomes.

title: Translational Profiling of Adult C. elegans Glia Using Translating Ribosome Affinity Purification (TRAP).
abstract: Glial cells are highly responsive to internal and external cues, so methods that accurately capture their molecular state are essential. However, standard transcriptomic workflows can distort native profiles, and transcript abundance does not always reflect what is ultimately translated into protein. Translational profiling helps address this gap by measuring the mRNAs actively engaged by ribosomes. Translating Ribosome Affinity Purification (TRAP) is a genetically targeted strategy that isolates translating ribosomes from specific cell types, enabling cell-type-resolved profiling of the translatome. Adapting this approach in C. elegans provides a useful way to profile glial translation programs and connect them to glia-driven regulation of organismal physiology.

title: Recent approaches to modulate citrinin biosynthesis in Monascus species: a review.
abstract: The filamentous fungi Monascus spp. are rich sources of secondary metabolites that include Monascus azaphilone pigments, monacolin K, and γ-aminobutyric acid, making them significant in the food, nutraceutical, cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries. Despite the industrial importance of this fungus, its production of citrinin, a nephrotoxic polyketide mycotoxin, remains a major drawback and limits its commercial application. Recent research studies have shown that the mechanism that governs citrinin biosynthesis highlights the interactions between Biosynthetic Gene Clusters (BGCs), epigenetic modifications, global regulatory networks, and environmental factors. The current understanding of the molecular and epigenetic mechanisms used to mitigate citrinin production in Monascus spp. is discussed in this review. Emphasis is given on histone acetylation and deacetylation, methylation, chromatin remodeling, the velvet complex, and the modulation of toxin biosynthesis through RNA-level gene expression control. The recent advances are critically evaluated for engineering citrinin-free strains, including transcriptomics, proteomics, multi-omics, RNA interference, CRISPR/Cas genome editing, and synthetic biology. The comparative analysis of these approaches shows that integrating epigenetic engineering with advanced genome and metabolic engineering can regulate citrinin while maintaining other important metabolite yields. Combining multi-omics and artificial intelligence-guided strain design with epigenetic interventions will accelerate the development of safe, sustainable, and high-yielding Monascus-assisted bioprocesses.

title: The miR-483-3p/METTL3/MMP9 Axis Regulates Schwann Cell Apoptosis and Autophagy in Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy.
abstract: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) is a prevalent and debilitating complication of diabetes with limited therapeutic options. The roles of epigenetic regulation involving microRNAs and RNA methylation in DPN remain poorly understood. This study aims to investigate the functional role and molecular mechanism of miR-483-3p in DPN, focusing on its interaction with the m6A methyltransferase METTL3 and its downstream target MMP9, thereby positioning METTL3 and MMP9 as potential therapeutic targets downstream of miR-483-3p. DPN models were established in vivo using a high-fat diet and streptozotocininduced diabetic rats, and in vitro using high-glucose (50 mM)-treated RSC96 Schwann cells (SCs). qPCR was used to measure miR-483-3p expression levels, and dual-luciferase reporter assays confirmed the interaction between miR-483-3p and METTL3. MeRIP-qPCR and RNA stability assays were employed to assess m6A modification and stability of MMP9 mRNA. Functional effects of miR-483-3p overexpression, alone or in combination with METTL3 or MMP9 overexpression, were evaluated by assessing nerve conduction velocity, thermal and mechanical thresholds, myelin structure with quantitative assessment of myelin thickness and abnormal fiber percentage, cell viability, apoptosis (flow cytometry and Western blot), and autophagy markers (Western blot). In both DPN rats and RSC96 cells treated with high glucose, miR-483-3p expression was notably reduced (p < 0.01). Overexpression of miR-483-3p markedly improved nerve function, reduced mechanical and thermal thresholds toward Sham levels, alleviated myelin abnormalities (as evidenced by reduced percentage of abnormal myelin fibers and increased myelin thickness), increased viability, reduced apoptosis, and restored alterations in autophagy-related protein expression (p < 0.01). Mechanistically, miR-483-3p directly targeted the 3'UTR of METTL3, suppressing its expression. METTL3 promoted MMP9 expression by enhancing m6A modification and stabilizing MMP9 mRNA. Experiments showed that increasing the expression of METTL3 or MMP9 counteracted the protective effects of miR-483-3p in both in vivo and in vitro, resulting in increased apoptosis, disrupted autophagy, and aggravated neuropathy (p < 0.01). Our findings identify a novel miR-483-3p/METTL3/MMP9 regulatory axis in DPN. The downregulation of miR-483-3p under hyperglycemic conditions relieves its suppression of METTL3, leading to increased m6A-dependent stabilization of MMP9 mRNA and subsequent impairment of apoptosis and autophagy. These results position miR-483-3p as a critical epigenetic regulator that links miRNA and RNA methylation pathways in DPN and further identify METTL3 and MMP9 as potential therapeutic targets warranting validation in human DPN samples. Limitations of this study include the need for clinical validation in human samples and further investigation of upstream regulators of miR-483-3p. This study demonstrates that miR-483-3p exerts protective effects against DPN by targeting the METTL3/MMP9 axis, thereby inhibiting apoptosis and promoting autophagy in SCs. Targeting the miR-483-3p/METTL3/MMP9 pathway represents a promising therapeutic strategy for DPN and warrants future clinical validation.

title: Targeting Long Non-Coding RNAs in Tau Phosphorylation: A New Paradigm for Diagnosis and Therapy in Tauopathies.
abstract: Tau phosphorylation is a critical regulatory process in neuronal physiology, and its dysregulation is a hallmark of tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease. While canonical protein kinases and phosphatases have been extensively studied as regulators of tau phosphorylation, long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have recently emerged as key epigenetic and post-transcriptional modulators of this process. This review comprehensively synthesizes current evidence on the mechanistic roles of lncRNAs in regulating tau phosphorylation. This study describes four primary mechanisms through which lncRNAs influence tau phosphorylation: (1) acting as competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs) to sponge microRNAs that target tau or tau-modifying enzymes, (2) functioning as natural antisense transcripts that modulate the expression of tau kinases, (3) modulating gene expression through epigenetic and transcriptional regulation, and (4) influencing protein activity and mRNA stability. This study further examines the cellular clearance of hyperphosphorylated tau via the ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy-lysosomal pathways and identifies the unexplored role of lncRNAs in these degradation processes as a critical knowledge gap. Finally, we discuss the translational potential of lncRNAs as non-invasive diagnostic biomarkers detectable in biofluids and as promising therapeutic targets for tauopathies. Understanding the intricate regulatory networks of lncRNAs in tau phosphorylation provides novel mechanistic insights into tau pathology and opens new avenues for diagnosis and therapeutic intervention in neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Multi-omics profiling suggests deep brain stimulation-associated expansion of CLIC3+ NK cells attenuates neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) alleviates Parkinson's disease (PD) symptoms, but its immunomodulatory mechanisms remain elusive. Through integrating microarray (GSE23676), single cell/nucleus RNA-seq (GSE184950, GSE202210, GSE223138, GSE243639; after quality control (mitochondrial gene content <25%, gene number >200) 616,076 high-quality cells were included), and GWAS data, we identified CLIC3 as a DBS-associated, potential protective implications in PD. CLIC3 was selectively up-regulated in a distinct natural killer cell subset (NK_CLIC3), which secreted TGFB1 to restrain neuroinflammation. CellChat and immunohistochemistry revealed that NK_CLIC3 cells communicated with PD-relevant neuronal populations: excitatory (SLC18A2+), inhibitory (SLC18A2+), oligodendrocyte (SLC18A2+), and astrocytic (SLC18A2+) cells via THY1-ADGRE5 and GZMA-PARD3 axes. Immune infiltration analysis (GSE114517; n = 75) suggested NK infiltration and deficient M2 macrophage recruitment in PD brains, underscoring an inadequate anti-inflammatory response. We further isolated CLIC3-positive NK cells (from a healthy donor) by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) and confirmed their ability to degrade α-synuclein, the pathological protein in Parkinson's disease, supporting the potential NK(CLIC3+) cells' protective function in PD. Our findings suggest DBS may expand NK_CLIC3 cells to suppress neuroinflammation through TGFB1 mediated immune-neuronal crosstalk, positioning CLIC3 as a prospective therapeutic target for PD.

title: SLC9A8 deficiency impairs the integrity of the intestinal mechanical barrier by inducing endoplasmic reticulum stress.
abstract: SLC9A8 contributes to intestinal barrier function, but its role in mechanical barrier integrity remains unclear. To elucidate the impact of SLC9A8 deficiency on mechanical barrier integrity and the underlying mechanisms. Wild-type and Slc9a8-/- mice received 2% DSS to induce colitis. Intestinal organoids and Caco-2 cells were used for in vitro studies. Paracellular permeability, western blot, SLC9A8 siRNA, SLC9A8 inhibitor (EIPA), and ER stress (ERS) inhibitor (4-PBA) were applied. Slc9a8-/- mice showed increased susceptibility to DSS-induced colitis with worsened mucosal barrier damage and inflammatory injury. Both in vivo and in vitro, SLC9A8 deficiency impaired mechanical barrier, evidenced by increased paracellular permeability and altered tight junction protein expression. RNA-seq and bioinformatics revealed significant ERS in Slc9a8-/- mice, confirmed by elevated IRE1α, GRP78, XBP1s, ATF6, ATF4, and Chop. 4-PBA inhibition of ERS significantly decreased Claudin-2, reduced FITC-dextran flux, and restored transepithelial electrical resistance in Caco-2 monolayers. SLC9A8 maintains intestinal mechanical barrier integrity by alleviating ERS.

title: NAT10-mediated ac4C RNA modification in disease: mechanisms and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C) is a conserved RNA modification associated with RNA stability, translation and cellular adaptation. N-acetyltransferase 10 (NAT10) modifies several RNA classes and also has functions that can be separated from RNA acetylation. Consequently, NAT10-dependent phenotypes do not by themselves establish a causal role for ac4C on a particular transcript. This review connects NAT10 structure and substrate recruitment with detection methods, disease mechanisms and therapeutic development. We distinguish site-resolved ac4C causality, transcript-associated acetylation with RNA-fate evidence, NAT10-dependent effects with unverified ac4C involvement, and pharmacological effects with unresolved target attribution. Evidence is traced from the modification event through RNA fate, pathway output and cellular-state maintenance to disease phenotype. Representative mechanisms are assessed individually, including separate genetic and drug-derived conclusions. We consider ac4C as a potential context-dependent post-transcriptional state stabilizer, rather than a universally activating or irreversible mark. Protective functions in germ cells and selected inflammatory responses constrain extrapolation from cancer. We critically assess Remodelin and emerging NAT10-directed compounds, distinguish catalytic inhibition from protein depletion, and discuss the assays, exposure measurements and pharmacodynamic markers needed for translation. Selective RNA acetylation inhibition and clinically validated ac4C biomarkers remain development objectives.

title: NtJAZ4 and NtHD12 co-regulate the stigma epidermal development in Nicotiana tabacum.
abstract: Homeodomain-leucine zipper IV (HD-Zip IV) family transcription factors play critical roles in plant epidermal development. However, their specific roles in the regulation of tobacco stigma epidermal development and the associated molecular mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, we investigated the core HD-Zip IV members that regulate stigma epidermal development in Nicotiana tabacum, and clarified the associated molecular mechanisms. The results demonstrated that a HD-Zip IV member (NtHD12) is endogenously associated with a jasmonate ZIM-domain (JAZ) protein (NtJAZ4), and that these two proteins have contrary functions in tobacco stigma epidermal development. RNA-seq analysis of NtHD12-KO in relation to their non-transformed counterparts plants (CK) revealed significantly differentially expressed genes that were mainly enriched in the phytohormone signal transduction pathway. Additionally, NtHD12 was found to regulate the expression of five and seven genes associated with the JA signaling pathway and stigma development, respectively. Notably, NtHD12-KO showed significantly downregulated epidermal development-related genes, and this phenomenon possibly contributed directly to the observed stigma epidermal development defects. Protein-protein interaction assays further confirmed that NtHD12 physically interacts with NtJAZ4 and phenotypic characterization revealed a highly similar developmental phenotype for stigma epidermis in NtHD12-OE and NtJAZ4-KO lines. Furthermore, NtJAZ4 has a negative regulatory effect on the activity of NtHD12. Collectively, these findings indicated that NtJAZ4 and NtHD12 co-regulate stigma epidermal development in Nicotiana tabacum, providing novel insights into the molecular regulatory networks underlying the development of tobacco stigma.

title: Molecular epidemiology, spike-protein evolution, antigenic variation, and experimental pathogenicity of G2c porcine epidemic diarrhea virus: a systematic review.
abstract: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) is a major cause of severe enteric disease and mortality in neonatal piglets. This systematic review aimed to synthesize current evidence on the molecular epidemiology, spike-protein variation, experimental pathogenicity, and control-related applications of the G2c lineage. Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed, and ScienceDirect were searched for peer-reviewed original studies published from 1 January 2020 to 31 May 2026. Of 78 records identified, 26 studies met the eligibility criteria. G2c was the most frequently assigned lineage in several national, multi-provincial, and regional PEDV datasets in China, particularly in Sichuan and Guangdong. However, its distribution was geographically heterogeneous, and G2a remained predominant in Guangxi. Contemporary G2c viruses exhibited extensive spike-protein variation, including substitutions, insertions, deletions, and predicted glycosylation changes in antigenically relevant regions. Cross-neutralization studies demonstrated strain-dependent antigenic differences, but consistent lineage-wide immune escape was not established. Experimental infections showed that natural G2c isolates caused acute watery diarrhea, dehydration, intestinal villous atrophy, high viral shedding, and, in some studies, substantial mortality in neonatal or suckling piglets. Heterogeneity in experimental design prevented reliable comparison of virulence among strains. Current evidence also supports the development of G2c-specific molecular diagnostics and several vaccine approaches, including cell-adapted candidates, maternal-immunity strategies, messenger RNA vaccines, and autogenous inactivated vaccines. Overall, G2c is an epidemiologically important and pathogenic PEDV lineage. Standardized classification, whole-genome surveillance, functional antigenic studies, matched challenge experiments, and heterologous vaccine-efficacy evaluations are needed to improve disease control.

title: WTAP regulates TRAF6 expression and vascular plasticity-associated phenotypes in experimental cell models.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a highly vascular malignancy characterized by marked tumor vascular plasticity. Vasculogenic mimicry (VM)-associated phenotypes have been linked to aggressive tumor behavior and reduced sensitivity to antiangiogenic therapy, but the epitranscriptomic mechanisms contributing to these phenotypes in HCC remain incompletely defined. This study examined whether Wilms tumor 1-associated protein (WTAP) regulates cell growth and vascular plasticity-associated phenotypes in experimental models through m6A-associated post-transcriptional regulation of TNF receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6). WTAP and TRAF6 expression was measured in HepG2 and BEL-7402 cells and the hepatocyte comparator using RT-qPCR and Western blotting. Gain- and loss-of-function experiments were performed to assess cell viability, wound closure, invasion, the ability of the examined cells to support vascular-like network formation in tumor cell-HUVEC co-culture, and the expression of vascular plasticity- and EMT-associated proteins. MeRIP-qPCR was used to evaluate m6A enrichment of TRAF6 transcripts, and an Actinomycin D chase assay was performed to assess TRAF6 mRNA stability. WT/MUT reporter assays, YTHDF1 RNA immunoprecipitation followed by qPCR (RIP-qPCR), and YTHDF1 depletion were used to examine additional aspects of TRAF6 regulation. Subcutaneous xenograft models were used to evaluate tumor growth and PAS-positive/CD31-negative VM-like structures. WTAP and TRAF6 were upregulated in the examined cells. WTAP overexpression enhanced cell viability, wound closure, invasion, tumor cell-supported vascular-like network formation, and vascular plasticity/EMT-associated molecular changes. WTAP manipulation altered TRAF6 mRNA abundance, m6A enrichment, and decay; its effect was greater on the WT than the MUT reporter. WTAP overexpression also increased TRAF6 RNA recovery in YTHDF1 immunoprecipitates. YTHDF1 depletion reduced the associated TRAF6 protein increase despite persistently elevated mRNA. TRAF6 knockdown attenuated WTAP-driven phenotypes and tumor growth, while TRAF6 overexpression partially rescued the effects of WTAP knockdown. PAS/CD31 staining provided qualitative evidence of VM-like morphology. WTAP contributes to the observed cellular and xenograft phenotypes, partly through TRAF6 post-transcriptional regulation associated with altered m6A enrichment and mRNA stability. YTHDF1 may regulate TRAF6 protein, but its role in mRNA stabilization remains unproven. The precise m6A sites and perfusion of VM-like structures remain unclear and warrant validation in clinically relevant HCC models and human specimens.

title: Bone marrow niche disruption via interferon gamma-mediated CXCL9/CXCL10 secretion after allogeneic transplantation.
abstract: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) is a significant complication of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Recent studies have elucidated the susceptibility of the bone marrow (BM) to GVHD, demonstrating a correlation between post-transplant cytopenia and BM niche impairment. However, the mechanisms underlying the damage to perivascular stromal cells, a critical element of the BM niche, remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of alloimmune responses on BM niche populations, identify the mechanism underlying BM niche disruption after allo-HSCT, and highlight the CXCL9/CXCL10-CXCR3 axis as a potential therapeutic target. Using murine allogeneic BMT models, we characterized hematopoietic and perivascular niche alterations by flow cytometry, confocal imaging, and single-cell RNA sequencing. The effects of inflammatory cytokines on stromal cells were examined using in vitro co-culture and cytokine-stimulation assays. The role of IFN-γ signaling was further evaluated using IFN-γ receptor-deficient recipients. Spatial interactions between T cells and perivascular niche cells were quantified by confocal imaging, and the functional contribution of CXCL9/CXCL10-CXCR3 signaling was assessed using the selective CXCR3 antagonist AMG487. This study demonstrated that direct niche cell damage by inflammatory cytokines, such as interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), and inflammatory T cell relocation within the BM owing to excessive CXCL9 and CXCL10 secretion from niche cells, which is induced by IFN-γ signaling, result in further damage to niche cells. Pharmacological blockade of CXCL9/CXCL10 signaling by a selective CXCR3 antagonist mitigated T cell localization close to BM niche cells, with a concomitant reduction in niche cell damage. These findings identify IFN-γ-driven inflammation and CXCL9/CXCL10-CXCR3-mediated T-cell localization as key mechanisms of perivascular niche disruption after allo-BMT. Targeting T-cell-niche interactions may provide a strategy to preserve BM niche integrity and promote hematopoietic recovery after allogeneic transplantation.

title: Uncovering Key Targets of Rhizoma Coptidis, Radix Scutellariae, and Cortex Phellodendri in the Treatment of Periodontitis through Integrated Network Pharmacology and Toxicology: A Study Leveraging Single-cell and Bulk RNA Sequencing Data.
abstract: Rhizoma Coptidis, Radix Scutellariae, and Cortex Phellodendri are used to treat periodontitis. This study integrated network pharmacology and network toxicology to elucidate their principal active compounds, key targets, and potential toxicity. Using network pharmacology, differential expression analysis, and machine learning algorithms, key genes were identified from the intersection of genes associated with the active compounds of the three herbs and genes differentially expressed in periodontitis. Concurrently, single-cell analysis was performed to identify critical cell types, and key targets were identified by assessing their enrichment and expression patterns within these cell types. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed on complexes formed by the key targets and active compounds. Finally, the potential toxicity of the key active compounds and their corresponding targets was evaluated. PLAT, SELE, IL1B, CXCL8, FOS, and MMP3 were identified as key genes associated with periodontitis and were significantly involved in inflammatory responses. CXCL8 emerged as a potential key target and was most highly expressed in macrophages, which were identified as a candidate cell type of interest. Integration of molecular docking and MD simulations showed that the CXCL8-quercetin complex underwent progressive structural stabilization and exhibited strong predicted binding affinity. The three herbs may exert therapeutic effects against periodontitis through multicomponent, multi-target, and multi-pathway mechanisms. These computational predictions require further experimental validation of their efficacy and safety. The study identified macrophages as a candidate cell type of interest and CXCL8 as a potential target associated with herbal-component-mediated macrophage inflammation. Quercetin and wogonin were identified as core active compounds within Rhizoma Coptidis, Radix Scutellariae, and Cortex Phellodendri, with computationally predicted respiratory toxicity risks. These findings provide computational insights for further investigation of the potential mechanisms and safety of these herbal components in periodontitis.
