title: Metformin promotes placental adaptation to hypoxic stress through mitochondrial and translational pathways.
abstract: Preeclampsia is a leading cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity worldwide, with no approved disease-modifying medical therapy. The disorder originates from placental insufficiency characterised by chronic hypoxia, oxidative stress, inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction within placental trophoblasts. Although metformin is widely used in pregnancy and has shown benefit in preeclampsia clinical trials, its mechanism of action including direct effects on placental protein synthesis and mitochondrial adaptation under hypoxic conditions remain poorly defined. Our aim was to determine how metformin modulates placental protein synthesis and mitochondrial function under physiological and hypoxic conditions relevant to placental dysfunction. Primary human placental trophoblasts were cultured under normoxic (8% O₂) or hypoxic (1% O₂) conditions and treated with metformin. Label-free quantitative proteomics was used to identify altered molecular pathways. Mitochondrial adaptation was assessed by analysis of mitochondrial dynamics markers, electron transport chain (ETC) complex expression, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. Metformin upregulated proteins involved in RNA processing, protein synthesis, and metabolism, while downregulating proteins associated with extracellular matrix organization and apoptosis. Under hypoxic conditions, metformin increased markers of mitochondrial fission and significantly upregulated ETC complexes I, II, and IV. These changes were associated with reduced cellular ROS levels. Importantly, enhanced protein synthesis occurred without activation of unfolded protein response pathways, indicating preservation of cellular homeostasis. Metformin enhances placental adaptation to hypoxic stress by coordinating protein synthesis and mitochondrial respiratory function while reducing oxidative stress. These mechanistic findings provide translational insight into how metformin may improve placental resilience and support its further evaluation as a therapeutic strategy for preeclampsia and other pregnancy complications driven by placental dysfunction. Not applicable. This study does not meet the NHMRC definition of a clinical trial.

title: Transcriptomic Signature-Guided EGFP Labeling of Alveolar Epithelial Cells via RNA Sensing in Mouse Lungs In Vivo and Human Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis Lung Slices Ex Vivo.
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing has revealed transient and disease-associated alveolar epithelial states that are difficult to access with conventional transgenic approaches. Here, we describe a programmable RNA-sensing workflow based on CellREADR [cell access through RNA sensing by endogenous adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR)] to couple a selected cellular RNA signature to enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) translation. The protocol covers sequence-encoded sensing RNA (sesRNA) design and cloning, in vitro validation of sesRNA-dependent EGFP expression in HEK293T cells, production and heparin-column purification of adeno-associated virus variant 6.2FF (AAV6.2FF), delivery to mouse lungs, and application to human idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) precision-cut lung slices (PCLS). Sensors targeting Sftpc, Pdpn, or Sprr1a can be used to label alveolar type 2, alveolar type 1, and injury-induced Krt8+ alveolar differentiation intermediate cells in mice and KRT17+KRT5- aberrant basaloid cells in humans, respectively. Because cell specificity is programmed by the sensor sequence rather than a cell type-specific promoter or newly generated mouse line, this approach can be rapidly adapted to emerging transcriptomic targets in both experimental mouse models and human lung tissues, enabling cross-species validation and translational investigation of disease-associated epithelial states. Key features • Programmable sesRNAs convert endogenous RNA signatures into ADAR-dependent EGFP translation without requiring a new transgenic mouse line. • Includes candidate sensor design, in vitro validation of target-dependent EGFP expression in HEK293T cells, and AAV6.2FF production and purification using a heparin column. • Supports in vivo labeling of AT2, AT1, and Sprr1a-positive transitional alveolar epithelial cells in mice. • Extends the workflow to human IPF PCLS for ex vivo assessment of SPRR1A-guided reporter expression in KRT17+KRT5- aberrant basaloid cells.

title: Glucocorticoid receptor regulates osteoblast differentiation in association with Map7d2 and Erk2 signaling.
abstract: The glucocorticoid receptor (GR) is an important regulator of skeletal homeostasis; however, the molecular mechanisms through which it regulates osteogenic differentiation remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of GR using two complementary primary murine osteogenic cell models, bone marrow stromal cells (BMSCs) and bone-derived primary osteoblasts, together with comparative transcriptomic analyses. GR depletion significantly impaired osteogenic differentiation in both cell preparations, as demonstrated by reduced alkaline phosphatase (Alp) activity and altered expression of osteogenic markers. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) revealed extensive transcriptional changes following GR knockdown, with 3,530 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in BMSCs and 4,657 in primary osteoblasts. Despite substantial differences in gene expression profiles of the two osteogenic cell models, pathway enrichment analyses revealed common biological processes, including MAPK signaling and cell migration. Comparative transcriptomic analysis further identified only 17 genes that were consistently regulated in the same direction in both cell preparations, among which Map7d2 emerged as a previously unrecognized GR-responsive candidate. Combined depletion of GR and Map7d2 partially restored cellular Alp activity and the expression of selected osteogenic markers compared with GR depletion alone. Western blot analysis further showed restoration of Erk2 phosphorylation and Alp protein expression following combined GR and Map7d2 depletion, demonstrating an association between the partial rescue of selected osteogenic readouts and restoration of Erk2 signaling. Together, these findings identify Map7d2 as a previously unrecognized GR-responsive candidate associated with Erk2 signaling and osteogenic differentiation. Our study reveals common molecular responses to GR depletion across two primary murine osteogenic cell models and provides new insights into the transcriptional and signaling networks underlying GR-regulated osteogenic differentiation.

title: Corrigendum to: The Role of Noncoding RNAs in the Prognosis and Diagnosis of Colorectal Cancer: An Emerging Biomarker.
abstract: Following publication of the article entitled "The Role of Noncoding RNAs in the Prognosis and Diagnosis of Colorectal Cancer: An Emerging Biomarker" [1], certain phrases and expressions were identified that were unclear or inconsistent with established scientific terminology. To ensure accuracy and clarity of the published record, these expressions have been corrected using appropriate terminology that more accurately conveys the intended scientific meaning. These corrections are limited to the wording and terminology of the affected passages and do not alter the data, results, scientific interpretations, or conclusions of the article. The specific corrections are provided below: Section: 1.5, Paragraph 1 Original text: The long non-coding RNA Linc00707 is another example of non-coding RNA dysregulation in tumor cells. A protein called linc00707, which has been linked to a number of biological processes, is elevated and eliminates miRNAs in mesenchymal in human bone marrow as well as in hepatocellular carcinoma, gastric illness, and bosom malignant growth. It does this via in-creasing osteogenesis, which causes hepatocellular carcinoma and its metastasis [55]. Corrected text: The long non-coding RNA Linc00707 is another example of non-coding RNA dysregulation in tumor cells. A protein called linc00707, which has been linked to a number of biological processes, is elevated and eliminates miRNAs in mesenchymal stem cells in human bone marrow as well as in hepatocellular carcinoma, gastric disease, and breast cancer growth. It does this via increasing osteogenesis, which causes hepatocellular carcinoma and its metastasis [55]. The original article has been updated accordingly. This corrigendum is published to ensure transparency and accuracy of the scholarly record. title: RIPK2 influences bone metastasis in prostate cancer through macrophage-tumor cell interaction: a mechanistic study.
abstract: Bone metastasis is a leading cause of mortality in prostate cancer (PCa) patients with limited treatment options. Myeloid-tumor cell interactions in the tumor microenvironment (TME) critically drive metastasis, but the mechanisms involved are poorly understood. Elucidating the myeloid-tumor cell crosstalk is crucial for developing novel anti-metastatic therapies. Myeloid and tumor cell subsets were identified through single-cell RNA sequencing and copy number variation (CNV) analysis. Key signaling axes between these subsets were identified through cell-cell communication analysis. Molecular biological experiments, including qRT-PCR, Western blot, and flow cytometry, were conducted to investigate the effects of RIPK2+ macrophages on malignant tumor cell phenotypes. RIPK2+ macrophages and disseminated tumor cells (DTCs) were enriched in tumor samples. DTCs exhibited high CNV scores and metastatic potential. RIPK2+ macrophages displayed unique antigen-presenting and immunoregulatory characteristics and engaged in high-intensity interactions with DTCs via the THBS1-CD47 signaling axis. In vitro, RIPK2 upregulated THBS1 and CD47, promoted their protein interaction, and enhanced PCa cell proliferation, migration, and invasion while repressing apoptosis. Revealed by single-cell sequencing and molecular biological experiments, RIPK2+ macrophages promote PCa bone metastasis through the THBS1-CD47 axis. The findings expand the understanding of myeloid-tumor cell interaction networks in the TME and provide a theoretical basis for developing TME-targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: RBP1-driven retinol metabolism in tumor-associated lymphatic endothelial cells orchestrates triple-negative breast cancer progression and lymphatic metastasis.
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive breast cancer subtype and is characterized by a high metastatic potential and limited treatment options. TNBC frequently metastasizes to lymphatic vessels and the presence of breast cancer cells in tumor-draining lymph nodes (LNs) is an important prognostic factor. Nevertheless, the molecular and metabolic reprogramming of TNBC-associated lymphatic vasculature remains poorly understood. A comprehensive single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of 44,000 endothelial cells from human breast tumor datasets was performed. RBP1, a retinol-binding protein, was identified as a metabolic gene highly and specifically upregulated in tumor-associated lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs). Then, RBP1 expression in human TNBC biopsies was assessed, and its association with LN status and overall patient survival was investigated in a cohort of 1,474 breast cancer patients. We further evaluated the in vivo relevance of RBP1 by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Rbp1 knockout in a pre-clinical TNBC mouse model. In vitro functional studies were performed using co-culture systems and RBP1-silencing in LECs. Finally, RBP1 mechanism of action in the lymphatic vasculature was determined by bulk-RNA sequencing and validated by applying different cellular and molecular approaches. Single-cell profiling revealed that the metabolic gene RBP1 was upregulated in LECs within the human breast tumor microenvironment. Further analysis showed that lymphatic RBP1 expression was associated with LN metastases, and correlated with poor prognosis and reduced survival in TNBC patients. In the pre-clinical TNBC mouse model, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Rbp1 knockout reduced lymphangiogenesis, tumor growth and metastatic burden, and increased necrosis. Moreover, functional assays demonstrated that direct co-culture of LECs with TNBC cells, or exposure to their secretome, induced lymphatic RBP1 upregulation and enhanced pro-lymphangiogenic activities, whereas RBP1 silencing compromised their biological, redox and metabolic properties. Mechanistically, bulk RNA sequencing of RBP1-silenced LECs combined with experimental validation revealed that RBP1, through its retinol-binding domain, modulates the VEGFR3 and NOTCH pathways, while also involving lipid mobilization. We define lymphatic RBP1 as a key "switch" that couples LEC metabolism to molecular programs, thereby driving tumor-associated lymphangiogenesis, breast tumor growth and lymphatic dissemination in TNBC. Our findings underscore the potential of RBP1 as both a novel prognostic biomarker and a tractable therapeutic target for blocking TNBC progression and lymphatic metastasis.

title: Integrating Long-Read Structural Variant Analysis with single-nucleus RNA-seq to Elucidate Gene Expression Effects in Disease
abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are a major source of genetic diversity, yet how they impact cell types in complex brain diseases remains largely unexplored, partially due to limitations of short-read sequencing. Here, we addressed this fundamental question in Parkinson's disease (PD). generating long-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data for 100 post-mortem brain samples from a PD cohort, constructing a high-confidence catalog of 74,552 SVs. To resolve their functional impact, we integrated single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from two brain regions from the same samples and focused functional analyses on SVs proximal to genes previously nominated as cis-regulated, potential causal targets of PD-associated GWAS loci. Using expression quantitative trait locus and allele-specific expression analyses, we uncovered SVs significantly associated with expression in specific cell types as well as effects shared across cell types. This study demonstrates the power of uniting long-read WGS with transcriptomics to uncover SVs underlying complex disease architecture with cell type resolution.

title: METTL16 licenses T cell expansion via m6A-independent translational control.
abstract: T cell expansion requires a rapid increase in protein synthesis, yet methyltransferase activity-independent functions of RNA-modifying enzymes remain poorly understood. Here, we identify METTL16 as a regulator of T cell translation and proliferation. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed elevated METTL16 expression in CD4+ T cells from patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Constitutive and inducible T cell-specific knockout models showed that METTL16 supports peripheral T cell homeostasis and activation-induced proliferation. A catalytically inactive METTL16 mutant restored proliferation in METTL16-deficient cells. METTL16 associated with the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3 complex and promoted global protein synthesis and translation of Myc and additional cell-cycle-associated transcripts. METTL16-deficient T cells showed impaired cell-cycle progression and failed to induce colitis after adoptive transfer. These findings uncover a methyltransferase activity-independent role for METTL16 in coordinating translation to support T cell expansion and intestinal inflammation.

title: FGFBP2 p.T186S mutation in tumor associated fibroblasts supports progression of pancreatic cancer through autocrine and paracrine mechanisms.
abstract: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive human tumors with an extremely poor prognosis. The tumor microenvironment is characterized by a complex network of cellular interactions, in which cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) play a pivotal role in the initiation and progression of the disease. Previously identified somatic cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) mutations may have functional consequences thereby affecting pancreatic cancer biology. One of the identified mutations of the fibroblast growth factor binding protein 2 gene (FGFBP2) causes replacement from threonine to serine (p.T186S). The aim of this study was to investigate how this mutation may affect fibroblast function, the tumor microenvironment and cancer progression. FGFBP2 p.T186S mutation harboring fibroblasts (FGFBP2MUT) and wild-type fibroblasts (FGFBP2WT) were analyzed for activation markers, viable cell numbers, and migration. PANC-1 pancreatic cancer cells were incubated with conditioned media from FGFBP2MUT and FGFBP2WT fibroblasts to assess viable cell numbers and signaling pathway activation. RNA sequencing was performed to identify differentially expressed genes. Furthermore, publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic datasets were analyzed to explore downstream molecular mechanisms. FGFBP2 p.T186S mutation harboring cells (FGFBP2MUT) displayed increased expression of activation markers and cytokines as compared to controls. FGFBP2MUT cells exhibited increased viable cell numbers and migration. Further, conditioned medium derived from FGFBP2MUT promoted growth of the pancreatic cancer cell line PANC-1 and resulted in increased activation of the ERK1/2 signaling pathway. RNA sequencing analysis of PANC-1 cells treated with conditioned media derived from FGFBP2MUT revealed upregulation of the ETS homologous factor (EHF) gene. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis showed that EHF was primarily expressed in tumor cells and regulated fibroblasts through the platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) signaling pathway. In addition, spatial transcriptomic analysis revealed a correlation between EHF expression and CAF markers ACTA2, POSTN, and COL1A1. Our study shows that the FGFBP2 p.T186S point mutation promotes fibroblast activation potentially influencing tumor progression by increasing the viable cell population of pancreatic cancer cells.

title: Human podocytes uniquely express CD47 to limit ITGAV-dependent TGF-β signaling for protection.
abstract: Podocyte injury is central to glomerular diseases, but protective mechanisms unique to human podocytes remain largely unknown. Integrin-associated protein (CD47) is a membrane protein with multiple functions, and it is absent in mouse podocytes but enriched in human podocytes. We investigated whether CD47 has a specific protective role in human podocytes. We analyzed CD47 expression in human and mouse podocytes using public single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets, cultured cells, and kidney biopsy samples from patients with glomerular disease. To explore potential roles of CD47 in human podocytes, we generated a humanized mouse model with podocyte-specific expression of human CD47 and evaluated glomerular injury in nephrotoxic serum- and adriamycin-induced experimental nephropathies. In addition, CD47 knockdown by siRNA was performed in cultured human podocytes and its effects were analyzed. CD47 is highly expressed in human, but not mouse, podocytes. However, in patients with glomerular disease, CD47 expression in podocytes is downregulated and inversely correlates with disease severity. Humanized mice with podocyte-specific expression of human CD47 exhibited attenuated glomerular injury in both nephrotoxic serum- and adriamycin-induced experimental nephropathies. Consistently, CD47 knockdown by siRNA was sufficient to induce injury in cultured human podocytes. These results demonstrate a protective effect of CD47 on human podocytes. Mechanistically, CD47 can bind to integrin αV (ITGAV) and likely disrupt its ability to activate the latent transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), thereby protecting podocytes from injury, including CDC42 downregulation, cytoskeletal disruption, and dedifferentiation under stress. CD47 operates as a previously unrecognized, human-specific protective machinery that limits TGF-β signaling likely through preventing the activation of latent TGF-β by ITGAV in podocytes. Its downregulation in glomerular diseases suggests that maintenance of CD47 expression may represent a potential therapeutic approach.

title: Integrated machine learning, single-cell RNA sequencing, and experimental validation for exploratory investigation of Fructus Aurantii in treating major depressive disorder.
abstract: Fructus Aurantii (FA), a Chinese herbal medicine, has been indicated to have antidepressant effects in our previous study. The potential mechanism of FA in the therapy of major depressive disorder (MDD) was explored through machine learning, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and experimental validation. We conducted differential analysis and WGCNA on the expression cohorts of MDD to determine differentially expressed genes and key module genes. FA-related targets were retrieved from multiple databases. Through the intersection of the aforementioned genes, candidate core targets were screened using the cytoHubba plug-in and machine learning methods. Subsequent analyses of these targets included clinical diagnostic evaluation, enrichment analysis, immune infiltration analysis, and molecular docking. scRNA-seq was used to explore the potential cellular mechanisms of MDD. Finally, RT-qPCR was employed to verify the gene expression level of the candidate core targets in the hippocampus. Four candidate core targets (ALOX5, PIK3CG, CHUK, and LRRK2) were determined using the cytoHubba plug-in and machine learning methods (LASSO regression, SVM-RFE, and Boruta). These targets exhibited notably elevated expression levels in the MDD group, and this finding was validated via RT-qPCR. The nomogram showed favorable value in clinical decision-making and diagnosis. Integrated analysis of signaling pathways and immune cells indicated that immune inflammation exerts an impact on MDD. Moreover, eosinophils and macrophages exhibited strong correlations with these targets and played crucial roles in immune inflammation. The active components of FA (limonin, auraptene, isosinensetin, nomilin, and luteolin) showed high binding affinity to these candidate core targets. Additionally, the expression of LRRK2 changed remarkably during the developmental stage of excitatory neurons. This research suggests that FA may exert its therapeutic effects through candidate core targets including ALOX5, PIK3CG, CHUK, and LRRK2, and key pathways associated with inflammation, immune dysregulation, and neuronal damage, providing a new perspective and important reference for subsequent MDD research and the development of therapeutic strategies.

title: Circulating miR-10b-5p drives Kawasaki vasculitis via endothelial reprogramming and nominates CXCL8 as an early diagnostic biomarker.
abstract: Kawasaki disease (KD) is an acute systemic vasculitis and the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children, yet no specific biomarker enables early diagnosis at emergency department presentation. We aimed to define the molecular mechanisms driving KD vasculitis and to identify a clinically actionable early diagnostic marker. Whole microRNA sequencing of buffy coat specimens from patients with KD and febrile controls identified 68 upregulated microRNAs, of which 13 were prioritized. Candidates were validated in two KD-like vasculitis mouse models, and miR-10b-5p was consistently elevated. Inhibition of miR-10b-5p by a miRCURY locked nucleic acid inhibitor attenuated aortic root inflammation in vivo. In human coronary artery endothelial cells from adult donors, miR-10b-5p directly suppressed marker of proliferation Ki-67 (MKI67) and chromobox 5 (CBX5), driving a transition from proliferative and metabolic programs toward a proinflammatory phenotype, as confirmed by single-cell and bulk RNA sequencing. Chromatin accessibility profiling revealed increased accessibility at the C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 8 (CXCL8) promoter, and motif analysis identified CCAAT enhancer binding protein alpha (CEBPA) as the key transcriptional activator; CEBPA knockdown abrogated miR-10b-5p-induced CXCL8 upregulation, and direct binding was confirmed by binding assays and chromatin immunoprecipitation. Serum CXCL8 was markedly elevated in patients with KD relative to febrile controls at first presentation before definitive diagnosis and declined significantly at the 8-week follow-up. Receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated diagnostic utility, with sensitivity and specificity of 83.3% at an optimal cut-off of 20.91 pg/ml. In conclusion, we define a miR-10b-5p-MKI67/CBX5-CEBPA-CXCL8 axis driving endothelial reprogramming and neutrophil-recruiting inflammation in KD and identify serum CXCL8 as a candidate biomarker for timely KD recognition.

title: Integrative machine learning analysis of bulk and single-nucleus RNA sequencing reveals key cell types and biomarkers driving MASH-associated fibrosis.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) increases the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer, with liver fibrosis being the primary determinant of adverse outcomes. However, the molecular mechanisms driving fibrosis progression in MASH remains incompletely understood. We integrated four bulk RNA-seq datasets into a merged cohort (MergeCohort) and analyzed one single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) dataset. Robust Rank Aggregation (RRA), WGCNA and machine learning were combined to identify core genes associated with MASH fibrosis. Additionally, we established MASH mice model induced by methionine-choline-deficient (MCD) diet, and further check the expression of hub genes through quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). Single-nucleus transcriptomic profiling of liver tissues from MASH patients across distinct fibrosis stages was investigated to delineate cellular heterogeneity, reconstruct intercellular communication networks, and characterize key transcription factors (TFs) as well as receptor-ligand interactions involved in MASH-associated fibrosis. Based on the MergeCohort, we detected two key gene network modules associated with fibrosis progression in MASH through WGCNA. By integrating machine learning algorithms, we discovered seven core genes (CAPN6, FAP, KRT23, SOX4, STMN2, TAGLN and VWF) showing favorable discriminatory capability for fibrosis stage, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.81 (95% CI 0.69-0.93) in a distinct external cohort. Moreover, CAPN6, FAP and KRT23 showed directionally consistent upregulation in the liver tissues of MASH mouse model induced by MCD diet. Subsequently, applying cell-type deconvolution analysis, we assigned the predominant cell types (hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), cholangiocytes, hepatocytes and macrophages) to the key WGCNA modules. At the single-nucleus level, we identified FGF13+ cholangiocytes and SAAs+ hepatocytes subpopulations. Transcription factor regulon analysis identified key TFs (CREB5 and STAT3), which may play potential regulatory roles in FGF13+ cholangiocytes and SAAs+ hepatocytes. Cell-cell communication analysis further revealed crucial ligand-receptor pairs between HSCs and FGF13+ cholangiocytes (VEGFA_NRP1 and APP_CD74 axes), SAAs+ hepatocytes and HSCs (RSPO3_LGR4 and IGF1_IGF1R axes), SAAs+ hepatocytes and macrophages (TNFSF14_TNFRSF14 and SELE_CD44 axes) associated with the progression of liver fibrosis in MASH. This combined approach defines molecular signatures related to MASH fibrosis that may inform the development of novel therapeutic strategies and serve as a tissue signature associated with advanced fibrosis in MASH.

title: Two Immune States in Ex Vivo Venetoclax-Resistant AML: Antigen- Presentation Silencing versus Checkpoint Exhaustion.
abstract: Venetoclax with a hypomethylating agent is standard therapy for older or unfit patients with acute myeloid leukemia, yet resistance is common, and its immune correlates are largely unmapped; prior studies profiled the immune compartment in one subgroup only. We asked whether ex vivo venetoclax resistance comprises more than one immune state, and whether any immune-cold state is associated with promoter methylation of antigen presentation. We analyzed 367 BeatAML patients with paired ex vivo venetoclax dose-response and RNA-sequencing data. A resistance signature was derived from differential expression, decomposed by non-negative matrix factorization and resolved using consensus clustering. Immune gene panels, reference-based deconvolution and Connectivity Map queries were applied; 173 TCGA-LAML samples with matched methylation data were projected onto the same structure. Resistance separated along a two-state immune axis: an immune-cold pole with low antigen-presentation and checkpoint expression, and a checkpoint-high, cytotoxic T-cell-in-filtrated pole (p < 1 × 10⁻⁵ across all eight panels). In the validation cohort, the cold pole exhibited the highest promoter methylation of MHC class I and class II genes, as well as checkpoint genes (q < 1 × 10⁻⁴). The cold phenotype was dissociable from the NPM1 mutation: NPM1-wildtype patients within it stayed cold relative to those elsewhere (q = 0.010). The cold pole is checkpoint-negative yet carries promoter hypermethylation of the genes that load and display antigen, which a PD-L1-based assessment would misread as an absent target. The association is correlative. Ex vivo venetoclax-resistant AML comprises at least two immunologically distinct states. Methylation of antigen-processing genes may warrant evaluation as a bi-omarker alongside checkpoint gene expression.

title: The clinical and biological significance of TBRG4 expression in prostate cancer.
abstract: Transforming growth factor beta regulator 4 (TBRG4), regulates mitochondrial RNA processing. TBRG4 has been implicated in the progression of several malignancies, but its biological function and clinical relevance in prostate cancer remain unclear. Publicly available data from The Cancer Genome Atlas prostate adenocarcinoma cohort and three Gene Expression Omnibus cohorts were analyzed. Differential expression was assessed independently in TCGA-PRAD, GSE88808, GSE46602, and GSE70768. Progression-free survival (PFS) was evaluated in TCGA-PRAD. External PFS analyses were conducted in GSE70768 and GSE46602 using the publicly available biochemical-recurrence status and corresponding follow-up time. Gain- and loss-of-function experiments were performed in PC3 and DU145 cells, which showed the highest baseline TBRG4 expression among the tested prostate cancer cell lines. A PC3 subcutaneous xenograft was used for in vivo validation. TBRG4 was upregulated in the analyzed PCa cohorts and cell lines and was associated with higher Gleason score, prostate-specific antigen level, and pathologic T category. High TBRG4 expression was associated with shorter PFS in TCGA-PRAD in univariable analysis [hazard ratio (HR), 2.138; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.180-3.872; P = 0.012], but not after multivariable adjustment (HR, 1.411; 95% CI, 0.771-2.582; P = 0.264). TBRG4 overexpression increased colony formation, migration, invasion, and wound closure and was accompanied by decreased E-cadherin and increased N-cadherin and vimentin expression. TBRG4 knockdown produced the opposite effects. High TBRG4 expression was associated with phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B/mechanistic target of rapamycin pathway enrichment, and TBRG4 manipulation was accompanied by changes in pathway-protein phosphorylation. TBRG4 knockdown also reduced PC3 xenograft growth. TBRG4 is upregulated across the evaluated prostate cancer cohorts and is associated with adverse clinicopathological features in TCGA-PRAD. Functionally, TBRG4 supports tumor growth and invasive phenotypes, accompanied by changes in PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling. Associations between TBRG4 expression and progression-free survival were observed in selected cohorts, suggesting that TBRG4 may represent a prognostic factor in prostate cancer.

title: Multi-omics and pharmacological analyses identify DDX60 as a candidate EGCG-engaged target in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is highly aggressive with limited available biomarkers, and discovering causative, functionally significant, and pharmacologically tractable targets is fundamental for new intervention strategies. By integrating Mendelian randomization, multi-cohort transcriptomic validation, single-cell analysis, and experimental pharmacology, DDX60 was identified as a key candidate gene associated with ESCC. The two-sample MR integrating eQTLGen, IEU OpenGWAS, and FinnGen datasets identified DDX60 as a key gene associated with esophageal cancer. Multi-omics utilizing TCGA, GTEx, cfDNA 5hmC profiling, and paired clinical ESCC specimens validated DDX60 expression in ESCC. Single-cell RNA-seq showed DDX60 enrichment in tumor-derived malignant epithelial cells versus matched normal epithelium. Epithelial cells expressing high DDX60 displayed enhanced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and interferon-response signatures, accompanied by a slightly elevated PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway score and progression along the malignant epithelial trajectory. Functionally, silencing DDX60 in ESCC cells increased apoptosis, decreased the phosphorylation of PI3K, AKT, and mTOR, and inhibited migration and invasion. These results demonstrated the role of DDX60 in ESCC progression. To explore potential pharmacological modulation of DDX60, PheWAS- and DSigDB-guided compound screening, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulation were performed, identifying epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG) as a candidate DDX60-associated compound. EGCG reduced ESCC cell viability, decreased the levels of DDX60 protein, and enhanced the thermal stability of endogenous DDX60 in cell-based CETSA assays. Analysis using DDX60-knockdown cells further suggested that DDX60 status may influence cellular responsiveness to EGCG. Conclusively, DDX60 demonstrated considerable potential as an exploitable target in ESCC, amenable to modulation by EGCG through the disruption of DDX60-associated oncogenic mechanisms.

title: Midkine identifies a Treg-enriched immune-evasive phenotype associated with poor outcomes in clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
abstract: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are critical mediators of immunosuppression in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), yet the tumor-intrinsic signals that drive Tregs activation and immune escape remain poorly understood. This study aimed to identify key drivers of epithelial-Tregs communication and elucidate their clinical and therapeutic relevance. We analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data using CellChat to map epithelial-Treg interactions. Candidate genes were prioritized through survival analyses and subsequently validated across bulk transcriptomic datasets, immunotherapy cohorts, and a prospective institutional ccRCC cohort. Immune infiltration, pathway enrichment, and genomic alterations were systematically characterized. Spatial associations were examined by multiplex immunofluorescence, while functional roles were evaluated using in vitro assays and an in vivo syngeneic mouse model treated with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1). Among epithelia-Tregs signaling candidates, midkine (MDK) emerged as a core ligand with strong prognostic relevance. MDK was markedly upregulated in ccRCC and associated with advanced tumor stage, aggressive histologic features, and unfavorable survival. High MDK expression defined a distinct immunogenomic phenotype characterized by increased Treg infiltration and altered mutation patterns. Elevated MDK expression was associated with poorer outcomes with PD-1 monotherapy and tyrosine kinase inhibitor monotherapy and showed a similar adverse trend with immune checkpoint inhibitor-based anti-angiogenic combination therapy. Spatial analyses confirmed co-localization of MDK-expressing tumor cells with forkhead box P3+ Tregs. Functionally, MDK promoted tumor cell proliferation and migration and was associated with poorer tumor control during PD-1 blockade in vivo. High MDK expression defines a Treg-enriched, immune-evasive ccRCC phenotype associated with aggressive tumor biology and unfavorable outcomes across both immunotherapy and targeted therapy settings. MDK may serve as a biomarker of adverse disease biology and a potential therapeutic target, although its predictive value for treatment selection requires further validation.
